A.explanation: Density alone is vague and in physics usually means mass per unit volume, not the count of electrons needed in $I = Anve$.

B.explanation: Number per unit time is already described by current $I$ itself, since $I$ is charge passing per second.

C.explanation: In $I = Anve$, $n$ is the number density, the number of conduction electrons per unit volume with unit $\text{m}^{-3}$.

D.explanation: A volume has unit $\text{m}^3$ and would not make $Anve$ give current in amperes.

hints: Look at the other symbols in $I = Anve$: $A$ is cross-sectional area and $v$ is mean drift velocity, so $Av$ relates to volume swept out per second.
Check homogeneity of units: $I$ is in $\text{C s}^{-1}$ and $e$ is in $\text{C}$, so $Anv$ must give $\text{s}^{-1}$ and $n$ must supply $\text{m}^{-3}$.
Compare the wording of the options: distinguish mass density from count per unit volume, and count per unit volume from count per unit time.
walkthrough: Identify the given equation $I = Anve$ for a metallic conductor, where $A$ is area in $\text{m}^2$, $v$ is mean drift velocity in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $e$ is charge per electron in $\text{C}$.
Recall the derivation idea: in time $t$ electrons drift distance $vt$, so the volume containing electrons that cross a section is $Avt$.
If $n$ is the number of free electrons in each $1 \text{ m}^3$, then total number crossing is $nAvt$ and total charge is $nAvte$.
Current is charge per time, so $I = nAvte / t = Anve$, which only works if $n$ has unit $\text{m}^{-3}$.
That quantity is called number density, stated as number of conduction electrons per unit volume. This is option C.
